69424.etyen: The lowercase form of W. The letter developed in medieval Latin-script writing from a doubled form of the letter represented in modern typography by ⟨u⟩ or ⟨v⟩, which were not yet consistently distinguished as separate letters. The doubled form was used to represent the Germanic sound /w/, for which Classical Latin had no separate letter, and gradually developed into the independent letter ⟨w⟩. Its Norwegian name, dobbelt-v (“double v”), refers to its shape and historical origin. / The uppercase form of w. The letter developed in medieval Latin-script writing from a doubling of the letter forms ⟨u⟩ or ⟨v⟩, which were not yet consistently distinguished as separate letters. The doubled form was used to represent the Germanic sound /w/ and gradually developed into a letter in its own right. Its Norwegian name, dobbelt-v (“double v”), refers to its shape and historical origin.

11056.etyen:
Compound of drøv (“cud”) + tygger (“chewer”), literally “cud chewer”. The first element, drøv (“cud”), is of uncertain deeper origin; compare older Danish drøff, dreff and Swedish dialectal dröp, related to a verb meaning “to chew again”. The second element is tygger (“chewer”), from tygge (“to chew”) + -er (“agent noun suffix”). Tygge is inherited from Old Norse tyggja (“to chew”) and tyggva (“to chew”), from Proto-Germanic *kewwaną (“to chew”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁- (“to chew”).

1004592.etyen:
Ultimately unknown. Peter Andreas Munch connected the name with a reconstructed verb *svirka, corresponding to Proto-Germanic *swerkaną (“to darken, become obscured”), reflected in Old English sweorcan (“to become dark, be obscured”). If this explanation is correct, the river name would have meant approximately “the dark one”.
Compare the Norwegian river names Surka, Svorka and Sverka, which Oluf Rygh assigns to the same stem.
